A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it is either not learning or learning far too slowly within the budget. At default settings that budget is only 131k steps, about 32 PPO updates. Two causes seem likely. (1) Sample starvation: fewer PPO epochs buy more environment steps. (2) Representation: an exact build needs the agent to know where a brick lands. That is the highest build layer under the footprint, and every cell the brick fills at that layer must be missing. The baseline mixes all layers into one flat 2D feature map, which makes per-layer checks hard to learn. I propose a small factorial: the baseline with a cheaper, sample-rich recipe; a per-layer network that pools over footprints at each layer z, with the default recipe; and the per-layer network with the new recipe. This separates the effect of the recipe from the effect of the architecture.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored exactly 0, and training success in the last 10% of training was also 0. That points to something more basic than seed noise. The agent never finishes a correct build even on training designs, so it never gets the exact-build bonus and never learns when to choose DONE. Each step is close to a bandit with dense reward, but whether a placement is right depends on its landing layer L, which is the maximum build height under the footprint. The brick is right when the target has every footprint cell at layer L and no missing target cell under the footprint gets sealed in. The 2D baseline mixes layers at its first layer. r1c2 only saw layers z−1, z and z+1, plus a column embedding that was not lined up with z, so it could not easily check for sealing. Next I test a per-(cell, layer) scorer that sees the whole column shifted so that layer z sits at a fixed position, with two PPO-epoch settings and an optional 3×3 context within each layer.

### Round 3
All six trials score 0 on dev, and none got a single exact build in the last 10% of training. That includes the generic baseline, two recipes (2 or 4 epochs) and three per-layer footprint scorers. So the results can't rank any idea, and seed noise isn't what's holding us back: nothing learns at all. Two explanations seem likely. (1) The world differs from the description, for example the action index is laid out differently (transposed, shifted anchor or permuted types). A purely local head, where the logit at cell (y,x) only sees nearby features, could never learn that, and every design so far has had such a head. (2) Learning is limited by samples, or the agent never learns when to choose DONE. This round hedges with three designs that can each learn an arbitrary mapping from positions to actions: a local+dense hybrid, a plain MLP with the most samples the budget allows, and a cell transformer with learned positional embeddings.

### Round 4
All nine trials, the starting network included, score 0 on both dev and training success. Very different networks (per-layer scorer, plain MLP, transformer) all failed, and so did the MLP's 426k steps, the most this budget allows. So neither network structure nor sample count seems to be the main cause. One factor has not been tested: the number of policy updates. The default recipe makes only about 32 PPO updates. Clipping caps how far the policy moves at each update, so 32 may be too few to go from near-uniform choices over 257 actions to a sharp policy. The 2-epoch runs were not much better (55 to 108 updates). This round tests many small updates: 1,024- or 512-step batches, giving about 160 to 260 updates. It also adds two network ideas: the legality mask as an input, and a deeper conv trunk that sees the whole grid with per-anchor outputs.
